title: PTAT Currents and Constant-Gm Biasing
intro: Some circuits need a current that grows with temperature, others a transconductance that does not change at all. Both come from small variations on the same self-biased loops (Razavi, Sections 12.4 and 12.5).

blocks.text: In every bandgap core the branch currents are $V_T\ln n/R$, so a PTAT current is a by-product. A dedicated generator uses a PMOS mirror on top of $Q_1$ and $R_1 + Q_2$, with an op amp equalising the two nodes:

An alternative replaces the op amp with the self-biased NMOS/PMOS mirror loop of the supply-independent reference, the pnp pair taking the place of the NMOS devices; the op-amp version gives better supply rejection and works at lower voltage. In both, mismatch and especially the temperature coefficient of $R_1$ bend the current away from the ideal PTAT line.
A bandgap from the PTAT current

blocks.alt: Schematic. Three PMOS transistors M3, M4 and M5 hang from VDD with their gates on one line driven by op amp A1. M3 feeds node X and the emitter of unit pnp Q1; M4 feeds node Y, then R1, then the emitter of pnp Q2 with n units. X goes to the op amp's minus input and Y to its plus input. M5 drives the output node Vout, from which R2 runs to the emitter of a third pnp Q3.
blocks.caption: Copy the PTAT current with $M_5$ and push it through $R_2$ on top of a third junction.

blocks.text: Here the op amp drives only gates (no resistive load), and the size of $Q_3$ is a free choice as long as the total slope is zero. Mismatch between the PMOS copies is now the main error source.

Noise, gain and speed depend on $g_m$ more than on current. Return to the $R_S$-defined self-biased reference: its current is $\propto 1/(\mu_n C_{ox} R_S^2)$, and substituting it into $g_m = \sqrt{2\mu_n C_{ox}(W/L)I_D}$ cancels the device parameters:

The transconductance is set by a resistor and a ratio, independent of supply, mobility and threshold; every device that copies this current with matching $V_{GS}$ conditions (same type, same current density) inherits the same $g_m$. What is left is the resistor: its process spread sets the accuracy, and a known resistor TC can be compensated with PTAT or bandgap techniques.

If an accurate clock is available, $R_S$ can be replaced by a capacitor $C_S$ switched at $f_{CK}$, whose average resistance is $1/(C_S f_{CK})$ (see the switched-capacitor chapter). Capacitors are better controlled in absolute value and have a far smaller TC than resistors, so the bias becomes more reproducible; a bypass capacitor $C_B$ smooths the switching ripple. The same trick gives an accurate voltage-to-current converter, $I = V_{REF}C_S f_{CK}$.

blocks.title: PTAT current over temperature
blocks.text: A PTAT generator uses $n = 8$ and $R_1 = 10$ kΩ (zero TC). Find the current at 300 K and at 400 K.

blocks.title: Current-based bandgap
blocks.text: In the PTAT-current bandgap, $n = 8$ and $|V_{BE3}|$ falls at 1.5 mV/K. What $R_2/R_1$ gives zero TC? With $|V_{BE3}| = 0.72$ V, what is $V_{REF}$?

blocks.title: Constant-gm with a switched capacitor
blocks.text: A constant-gm bias uses $K = 4$ and needs $g_{m1} = 0.2$ mS. Find $R_S$. If $R_S$ is replaced by a switched capacitor clocked at 100 MHz, what $C_S$ is needed?
